title: US Drafts Chinese Data Center Ban, Chinese Telecoms Found Still Embedded in US Networks, CXMT IPO Reshapes Memory Chip Race
subhead: The FCC is preparing to block new Chinese optical transceivers from US data centers, while a House probe reveals three state-owned Chinese carriers never left American networks after FCC revocations — and China's CXMT surges to a $545B valuation as its DRAM market share explodes 716%.

sections.heading: FCC Drafts Ban on Chinese Data Center Optical Transceivers
sections.body:
The Trump administration is drafting a ban on US imports of new models of Chinese optical transceivers, the fiber-optic components that shuttle data between servers at light speed inside AI data centers, according to a Reuters exclusive citing four people familiar with the matter. The Federal Communications Commission is leading the measure, with officials hoping to publish it before year-end.

The target is Zhongji Innolight, which holds roughly 27% of the global data center transceiver market and generates 90% of its revenue outside China, according to Counterpoint Research. The Pentagon added Innolight to its list of alleged Chinese military-backed companies in June. The proposed rule would ban all new Chinese transceiver models from import, then exempt non-Chinese suppliers — a pattern the FCC has already applied to Chinese drones, routers, robots, and power inverters.

US-based transceiver makers Lumentum, Coherent, and Applied Optoelectronics surged 7%, 11%, and 18% on the news. But both the Foundation for American Innovation and industry analysts note that current US alternatives lack the scale to replace Chinese vendors at volume, raising cost concerns for cloud providers like Amazon Web Services that depend on Innolight components.

China's embassy in Washington warned that Beijing 'will take all necessary measures in response to any action that causes material harm to its interests.' The move reflects a deliberate effort to avoid a repeat of the Huawei experience, where equipment became so deeply embedded that removal proved slow and expensive.
sections.whyItMatters: This extends the US-China tech decoupling from chips into the plumbing of AI infrastructure itself. Optical transceivers are a $10B+ market and growing fast with AI buildouts — blocking the dominant Chinese supplier creates a near-term supply gap but signals Washington will preemptively block Chinese components before they become entrenched.

sections.heading: House Probe: Chinese Telecoms Never Left US Networks After FCC Revocations
sections.body:
A bipartisan House China Committee investigation released Tuesday found that China Telecom, China Mobile, and China Unicom retained equipment, data-center space, and network connections in the United States years after the FCC revoked their authorizations between 2019 and 2022. The nearly 50-page report, first seen by Nextgov/FCW and Defense One, reveals that FCC license revocations did not require the companies to remove equipment, vacate data centers, or sever private network links.

The carriers continued offering enterprise networking and internet transit services. The committee identified nearly 109,000 Border Gateway Protocol hijack incidents from January 2018 through May 2025 in which Chinese or Hong Kong-linked networks claimed US internet addresses without authorization, potentially diverting American traffic through their systems. More than 4,200 involved China Mobile-controlled networks.

The probe's most striking finding links to Salt Typhoon, the Chinese espionage campaign uncovered in 2024 that breached major US carriers and accessed wiretap systems. During September 22–25, 2024 — just as Salt Typhoon became public — China Mobile International's network appeared in routes to Salt Typhoon servers at least 192 times, helping keep attacker infrastructure reachable while US defenders tried to shut it down. The committee stops short of alleging China Mobile employees knowingly participated.

The committee recommends giving federal agencies authority over equipment and private network arrangements that persist after license revocations, along with targeted removal funding and stronger BGP routing protections. Telecom security expert Marc Rogers warned that the proposals would only work if countries act together: 'If only one country takes a strong position, China will just maneuver around them.'
sections.whyItMatters: The finding that revocation without removal is essentially meaningless reveals a fundamental gap in US telecom security policy. Three state-owned Chinese carriers maintained physical and network footholds for years after being told to leave, and their infrastructure was coincidentally present in the routing of the largest known Chinese espionage campaign against US telecoms.

sections.heading: CXMT's $545 Billion IPO Reshapes Global Memory Chip Market
sections.body:
China's CXMT, the country's largest memory chipmaker, saw its shares surge as much as 472% on its STAR Market debut, reaching a valuation of 3.68 trillion yuan ($544.9 billion) and making it mainland China's largest IPO in years. The company raised at least 8.6 billion yuan in the offering.

According to Counterpoint Research's Q2 report, CXMT's DRAM market share surged 716% year-on-year to 7%, making it the world's fastest-growing memory supplier. The growth was driven by rising demand for domestic substitution in critical infrastructure and enterprise IT, as well as market opportunities created by global suppliers shifting capacity toward high-bandwidth memory production.

The IPO's scale has direct implications for South Korea's dominance. Samsung reclaimed the DRAM top spot with 39% market share in Q2, while SK Hynix fell to 26% from 39% a year earlier despite a 214% revenue surge. CXMT's expanding DDR5 products for AI servers are becoming increasingly competitive, and Counterpoint Vice President Neil Shah noted that if CXMT can expand capacity for Tier-1 international customers, 'the supplier's market share will balloon and look a lot different a year from now.'

Eight Chinese banks held a combined 4.5% stake in CXMT before the IPO, underscoring the state-backed financing behind China's chip push. The company reports nearly 7,000 patents and over 20.6 billion yuan in R&D spending over the past three years.
sections.whyItMatters: CXMT's meteoric rise from niche player to $545B-valued competitor compresses the timeline for China's memory chip self-sufficiency. A 716% market share surge in one year signals that US export controls on HBM may be accelerating Chinese investment in alternatives rather than containing them — and the IPO proceeds give CXMT the war chest to close the technology gap faster.

sections.heading: 25 States Sue Over Trump's Forced-Labor Tariffs Covering 99% of US Imports
sections.body:
A coalition of 25 states led by New York filed suit Monday against the Trump administration over tariffs of 10–12.5% imposed on 59 countries and the EU using Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, covering roughly 99% of American imports. The states argue the forced-labor rationale is a pretext to replace tariffs that the Supreme Court struck down in February when it ruled the International Emergency Economic Powers Act did not authorize tariffs.

The lawsuit, filed in the Court of International Trade, marks the third legal challenge to the Section 301 tariffs, following two suits by small businesses represented by the Liberty Justice Center. New York Attorney General Letitia James called the tariffs 'an illegal attempt to raise taxes on families and businesses' after the Supreme Court loss.

The White House defended the tariffs, stating that 'Section 301 tariffs have proven to be a legally durable tool since the President's first term.' Law professor Barry Appleton noted that while previous tariff statutes were novel uses, Section 301 has been used for decades with 'real guardrails: investigation, consultation, a public record' — making this a real legal fight, not a formality.

Separately, the administration has invoked Section 338 of the US Tariff Act to apply additional tariffs on Canadian goods effective August 19, with a maximum of 50% on countries deemed to discriminate against US industry — and these would not exempt CUSMA-compliant goods.
sections.whyItMatters: The legality of the Section 301 forced-labor tariffs will determine whether the Trump administration has found a durable legal pathway for sweeping import duties after its IEEPA approach was struck down. If the courts uphold these tariffs, they create a permanent trade barrier affecting virtually all US imports — and if they don't, the administration's entire tariff architecture collapses.

sections.heading: Anthropic's $10B Norway Deal Brings Wall Street Credit Into the AI Infrastructure Stack
sections.body:
Anthropic signed a $10 billion, six-year compute procurement agreement with Volta Infra Holdings — a startup founded in January 2026 — for 121 IT megawatts of Nvidia Vera Rubin capacity at Bitdeer's Tydal data center campus in Norway. Bitdeer disclosed a 16-year, $4.7 billion colocation lease with Volta, with an optional eight-year renewal bringing the potential total to $8 billion over 24 years.

The deal's financial architecture is the real story: JPMorgan affiliates and a second global institution provided a $1.3 billion standby letter of credit backing Volta's payment obligations to Bitdeer. This credit backstop mirrors the function that Google's $43.8 billion in data center lease guarantees performs for the TPU ecosystem — but it is the first time JPMorgan-level institutional credit has directly supported Nvidia-ecosystem GPU deployments.

Volta is not a data center operator. It assembles the capital stack, credit support, and institutional financing that allows frontier AI labs to access GPU capacity without arranging infrastructure financing on their own balance sheet. CEO Ricard Boada, formerly of Brookfield Asset Management, described compute as 'a new infrastructure asset class' — language that positions GPU clusters alongside railways and power plants as investable infrastructure.

The Vera Rubin NVL72 rack packs 72 Rubin GPUs and 36 Vera CPUs in a fully liquid-cooled chassis, with a full 40-rack POD scaling to 1,152 GPUs and 60 exaflops. Tydal's Nordic hydroelectric power targets a PUE of 1.1 — roughly 48 MW less overhead than a comparable US data center running at 1.5 PUE.
sections.whyItMatters: This deal introduces institutional bank credit into the Nvidia GPU ecosystem's financing chain, closing the cost-of-capital gap that has given Google's TPU ecosystem a structural advantage. If JPMorgan-style credit backstops become standard for GPU deployments, it changes the economics of who can afford to compete in frontier AI compute — and how quickly non-hyperscaler capacity can scale.

sections.heading: US Heavy Rare Earth Plant Begins Construction in Utah
sections.body:
Energy Fuels has begun construction on a commercial-scale heavy rare earth metals plant at its White Mesa Mill in Utah — the only fully licensed and operating conventional uranium processing facility in the United States. The $104 million expansion will add production of terbium, dysprosium, samarium, europium, and gadolinium, with terbium and dysprosium online by end of 2027 and the rest by end of 2028.

Heavy rare earths are the critical pinch point in Western permanent magnet supply chains. The elements provide the coercivity and heat resistance that make magnets viable for EV motors, military systems, and data center hardware. China currently dominates their production.

The expansion is sized to process monazite from Energy Fuels' Donald Project joint venture in Australia, expected to deliver 8,500–9,500 tons of concentrate annually starting in 2028. Further expansions planned for 2029 would support a mine-to-magnet chain producing 15,700 tons of rare earth permanent magnets annually once pending acquisitions of Australia's Strategic Materials and Germany's Vacuumschmelze close — enough for millions of EVs, robots, or wind turbines.

The project is supported by a conditional $725 million US government loan commitment and fits into the Pentagon's broader campaign of direct equity stakes in MP Materials, price guarantees, and the $10 billion Project Vault strategic reserve. Energy Fuels CEO Ross Bhappu emphasized that government floor prices are 'vitally important' during loan repayment periods when Chinese market flooding could otherwise bankrupt new entrants.
sections.whyItMatters: For decades the US had no domestic heavy rare earth processing capacity. The White Mesa expansion, paired with Australian feedstock and German magnet manufacturing, creates the first integrated Western mine-to-magnet supply chain for the elements that make advanced magnets work — directly challenging the chokepoint China has held since the 2010 Senkaku incident.

sections.heading: Türkiye: Defense Exports Hit Record $5.79B in Seven Months
sections.body:
Türkiye's defense and aviation exports reached $5.79 billion in the first seven months of 2026, with the 12-month rolling total hitting $11.2 billion, according to the Turkish defense industry authority. The figures continue a sharp upward trajectory driven by demand for Turkish drones, armored vehicles, and naval platforms — particularly from Central Asian, African, and now Southeast Asian buyers.

ASEAN formalized upgraded ties with Türkiye this week, with discussions on defense industrial partnerships and expanded aviation links. The diplomatic upgrade comes as Türkiye seeks to convert its growing defense export portfolio into deeper industrial cooperation with regional partners.

Türkiye's defense export growth reflects a broader pattern: countries previously dependent on Western or Russian suppliers are turning to Turkish platforms as affordable, combat-proven alternatives. Bayraktar TB2 drones in Ukraine, Libya, and Ethiopia, along with MMC/STM naval platforms, have become reference points for buyers evaluating alternatives to pricier American and European systems.
sections.whyItMatters: Türkiye is transitioning from a defense import substitute to a genuine arms export competitor, with annualized exports approaching $10B. The ASEAN upgrade signals that Turkish defense industrial capability is becoming a factor in regional security architectures well beyond the Middle East — a tech-power angle that matters as supply chain sovereignty gains strategic weight.

bottomLine: The US-China technology contest entered a new phase on August 4-5: Washington is now targeting the fiber-optic plumbing inside AI data centers, while discovering that previous telecom revocations left Chinese state carriers physically embedded in American networks for years. Meanwhile, CXMT's $545B IPO and 716% market share surge shows that export controls may be accelerating China's self-sufficiency push as much as constraining it. The Anthropic-Volta-JPMorgan deal in Norway signals that institutional finance is finally entering the GPU infrastructure stack, and the Utah rare earth plant breaks ground on the first Western heavy rare earth supply chain. Twenty-five states are now challenging the legal framework for tariffs covering 99% of US imports — the outcome will shape whether the current trade architecture endures or collapses.
